traditions/early-church/summary: The undivided communion of churches from Pentecost through the era of the first ecumenical councils, before the lasting divisions of Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451). Nearly every later tradition claims continuity with it, whether through apostolic succession, doctrine or a restored pattern of worship. It was not uniform: Greek, Latin, Syriac and Coptic churches developed distinctive liturgies and theologies within a shared episcopal network.
traditions/early-church/distinctives/0: Communion of local churches led by bishops, presbyters and deacons
traditions/early-church/distinctives/1: Baptism and Eucharist at the centre of community life
traditions/early-church/distinctives/2: The 'rule of faith' and the gradual recognition of the New Testament canon
traditions/early-church/distinctives/3: Synods and ecumenical councils to settle disputes
traditions/early-church/distinctives/4: Veneration of martyrs and, from the fourth century, monasticism
traditions/early-church/profile/authorit: Scripture (the Septuagint and apostolic writings) read within the apostolic tradition handed down by bishops in succession and articulated in creeds and councils.
traditions/early-church/profile/salvatio: Salvation through Christ's death and resurrection, received in faith and baptism and lived out in the church; Eastern writers stressed deification, Western ones increasingly grace and sin.
traditions/early-church/profile/sacramen: Baptism (usually with anointing) and the Eucharist as the central 'mysteries', with penance for serious post-baptismal sin and ordination of clergy.
traditions/early-church/profile/eschatol: Expectation of Christ's return, bodily resurrection and judgment; some (e.g. Papias, Irenaeus) held to an earthly millennium, others (Origen, later Augustine) read it spiritually.
traditions/early-church/profile/governan: Monarchical episcopate emerging by the second century, with metropolitan and patriarchal sees (Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, later Constantinople and Jerusalem) gaining precedence.
traditions/early-church/profile/worship: Sunday Eucharist with Scripture readings, prayers, psalms and hymns; catechumenate and Easter baptism; increasingly fixed liturgical families by the fourth century.
traditions/early-church/profile/canon: The Old Testament largely in its Greek (Septuagint) form; a New Testament core of Gospels and Pauline letters by c. 200, with Athanasius' Festal Letter (367) listing the 27 books.
traditions/early-church/status: Historical; its communion divided after Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451), with successor churches all claiming its heritage.
traditions/montanist/summary: A prophetic movement begun in Phrygia by Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla, who claimed the Paraclete spoke directly through them. It called for stricter discipline, fasting and readiness for martyrdom, and expected the New Jerusalem to descend at Pepuza. Condemned by Asian synods, it nevertheless attracted Tertullian in North Africa and survived in Phrygia until suppressed in the sixth century.
traditions/montanist/distinctives/0: Ecstatic prophecy as continuing revelation of the Paraclete
traditions/montanist/distinctives/2: Rigorist ethics: fasting, no remarriage, no flight from persecution
traditions/montanist/distinctives/3: Expectation of the New Jerusalem at Pepuza
traditions/montanist/profile/authority: Scripture and the apostolic faith, supplemented by the oracles of the New Prophecy, regarded as the Paraclete's fuller guidance.
traditions/montanist/profile/salvation: Broadly shared the church's teaching, with heightened stress on holiness and steadfastness under persecution.
traditions/montanist/profile/sacraments: Baptism and Eucharist as in the wider church; serious post-baptismal sins were considered beyond the church's power to forgive.
traditions/montanist/profile/eschatology: Imminent end, with the heavenly Jerusalem expected to descend at Pepuza in Phrygia.
traditions/montanist/profile/governance: Leadership by prophets alongside a hierarchy including 'patriarchs' and 'koinonoi' at Pepuza, according to later reports.
traditions/montanist/profile/worship: Assemblies featuring ecstatic prophecy; strict fasts; women were reportedly admitted to clerical roles.
traditions/montanist/profile/canon: Accepted the church's Scriptures; collections of the prophets' oracles circulated, alarming critics who feared an expanded canon.
traditions/montanist/status: Extinct; suppressed by Justinian's legislation in the sixth century.
traditions/marcionite/summary: Founded by Marcion of Sinope, excommunicated at Rome c. 144, who taught that the God of the Old Testament, a just creator, was distinct from the good, merciful Father revealed by Jesus. He rejected the Hebrew Scriptures and compiled a canon of an edited Luke and ten Pauline letters. His well-organised church spread widely and survived in Syria into the fifth century and later.
traditions/marcionite/distinctives/0: Distinction between the Creator-God of the Law and the higher God of love
traditions/marcionite/distinctives/2: First known fixed Christian canon (Gospel and Apostle)
traditions/marcionite/distinctives/3: Strict asceticism, including celibacy for the baptised
traditions/marcionite/profile/authority: Marcion's edited Gospel and ten Pauline letters, read as the uncorrupted message of Paul, along with Marcion's Antitheses.
traditions/marcionite/profile/salvation: Rescue by the alien, good God from the dominion of the Creator through faith in Christ, who appeared without being born.
traditions/marcionite/profile/sacraments: Baptism (only for the celibate) and a Eucharist reportedly using water rather than wine.
traditions/marcionite/profile/eschatolog: No future reign of the Creator's Messiah; the saved are taken into the realm of the good God.
traditions/marcionite/profile/governance: Bishops and presbyters on the catholic model, forming a parallel church network.
traditions/marcionite/profile/worship: Assemblies similar to those of the wider church, marked by rigorous asceticism.
traditions/marcionite/profile/canon: The 'Evangelion' (an edited Luke) and 'Apostolikon' (ten Pauline letters, excluding the Pastorals).
traditions/marcionite/status: Extinct; declined after the fourth century, with remnants in Syria and Persia possibly into the tenth.
traditions/gnostic/summary: A diverse range of second-century teachers and groups—Valentinians, 'Sethians', Basilideans and others—who taught that salvation comes through secret knowledge (gnosis) of the soul's divine origin. Most distinguished the true God from an inferior creator (the demiurge) and viewed the material world as flawed. Known mainly through critics like Irenaeus until the Nag Hammadi discovery (1945); modern scholars debate whether 'Gnosticism' names a single movement.
traditions/gnostic/distinctives/0: Salvation through revealed knowledge of one's divine origin
traditions/gnostic/distinctives/2: A lesser creator responsible for the material world
traditions/gnostic/distinctives/3: Esoteric interpretation of Scripture and secret traditions
traditions/gnostic/distinctives/4: Spiritual elite distinguished from ordinary believers (in some systems)
traditions/gnostic/profile/authority: Secret apostolic traditions and revelations (e.g. Gospel of Truth, Apocryphon of John) alongside allegorically read Scripture.
traditions/gnostic/profile/salvation: Awakening of the divine spark through gnosis imparted by a heavenly Redeemer, enabling the soul's return to the Pleroma.
traditions/gnostic/profile/sacraments: Varied: Valentinians practised baptism, chrism, Eucharist and a 'bridal chamber' rite (Gospel of Philip).
traditions/gnostic/profile/eschatology: Ascent of the spirit beyond the cosmic powers; rejection or reinterpretation of bodily resurrection.
traditions/gnostic/profile/governance: Mostly teacher-centred circles, often meeting within or alongside catholic congregations.
traditions/gnostic/profile/worship: Initiation rites, study and contemplative ritual; details vary greatly by group.
traditions/gnostic/profile/canon: Used many of the church's writings plus their own gospels and revelation dialogues, many preserved in Coptic at Nag Hammadi.
traditions/gnostic/status: Extinct as organised Christian movements by c. 500; Mandaeism and Manichaeism are related but distinct religions.
traditions/arian-homoian/summary: Arius of Alexandria taught that the Son, though divine and pre-existent, was created by the Father and not co-eternal ('there was when he was not'). Condemned at Nicaea (325), related views gained imperial favour in the mid-fourth century, and the Homoian creed ('the Son is like the Father') of 359–360 was adopted by the Goths through Ulfilas. Rejected at Constantinople (381), Homoian Christianity remained the faith of the Goths, Vandals and Lombards until their conversions to Nicene faith, Visigothic Spain renouncing it at Toledo in 589. 'Arian' was largely a label applied by opponents to diverse parties.
traditions/arian-homoian/distinctives/0: The Son as the first and highest creature, subordinate to the Father
traditions/arian-homoian/distinctives/1: Rejection of homoousios ('of the same substance')
traditions/arian-homoian/distinctives/2: Homoian formula: the Son is 'like' the Father according to the Scriptures
traditions/arian-homoian/distinctives/4: Identity marker of Germanic ruling elites in the West
traditions/arian-homoian/profile/authori: Scripture, with suspicion of non-biblical terms such as ousia in creeds.
traditions/arian-homoian/profile/salvati: Salvation through the Son as mediator, the obedient and exalted Word through whom the Father created and redeems.
traditions/arian-homoian/profile/sacrame: Baptism and Eucharist; baptism was sometimes administered in the name of the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.
traditions/arian-homoian/profile/eschato: Shared the general Christian expectation of resurrection and judgment.
traditions/arian-homoian/profile/governa: Episcopal, with bishops often attached to Gothic and Vandal royal courts.
traditions/arian-homoian/profile/worship: Liturgy in Greek, Latin or Gothic; distinct churches alongside Nicene ones in barbarian kingdoms (e.g. in Ravenna).
traditions/arian-homoian/profile/canon: The common Scriptures; Ulfilas' Gothic translation reportedly omitted the books of Kings as too warlike.
traditions/arian-homoian/status: Extinct; the last major Homoian kingdom, the Lombards, adopted Nicene faith in the seventh century.
traditions/donatist/summary: A North African church that arose after the Diocletianic persecution, refusing to accept Caecilian as bishop of Carthage because one of his consecrators was alleged to have surrendered Scriptures (traditio). Named after Donatus, its bishop of Carthage, it held that sacraments administered by unworthy clergy were invalid and that the true church must be pure. Opposed by Augustine and imperial coercion after the Conference of Carthage (411), it persisted until the Arab conquest.
traditions/donatist/distinctives/0: A pure church of the martyrs, uncontaminated by 'traditors'
traditions/donatist/distinctives/1: Validity of sacraments dependent on the holiness of the minister
traditions/donatist/distinctives/2: Rebaptism of converts from the catholic church
traditions/donatist/distinctives/4: Strong regional Punic and Berber popular base
traditions/donatist/profile/authority: Scripture and the tradition of Cyprian of Carthage, especially his teaching that there is no valid baptism outside the true church.
traditions/donatist/profile/salvation: Salvation within the holy, persecuted church of the martyrs, separated from compromise.
traditions/donatist/profile/sacraments: Baptism and Eucharist valid only when performed by clergy in the pure church; catholic baptism was repeated.
traditions/donatist/profile/eschatology: Shared expectation of judgment; martyrdom seen as a direct path to glory.
traditions/donatist/profile/governance: Episcopal, with rival bishops in hundreds of North African towns; at its height the larger church in Numidia.
traditions/donatist/profile/worship: Latin liturgy similar to that of the catholics, with fervent martyr cults; the Circumcellions were a radical associated group.
traditions/donatist/status: Extinct; disappeared with North African Latin Christianity after the Arab conquest (late seventh century).
traditions/oriental-orthodox/summary: A communion of six autocephalous churches—Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Armenian, Syriac and Malankara (Indian)—that accept the first three ecumenical councils but not Chalcedon (451). They confess, following Cyril of Alexandria, 'one incarnate nature of God the Word', a Miaphysite position (called Monophysite by opponents) that they distinguish from the Eutychian heresy they also reject. Modern dialogues with Eastern Orthodox and Catholics have concluded that the Christological differences are largely terminological.
traditions/oriental-orthodox/distinctive: Miaphysite Christology: one united divine-human nature of Christ
Recognition of three ecumenical councils (Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus)
Ancient liturgical languages: Coptic, Ge'ez, Classical Armenian, Syriac
Rich monastic and martyr traditions under centuries of non-Christian rule
Communion among churches of very different cultures without a single primate
traditions/oriental-orthodox/profile/aut: Holy Scripture within Holy Tradition, as interpreted by the Fathers (especially Cyril and Dioscorus) and the three councils.
traditions/oriental-orthodox/profile/sal: Deification and salvation through union with the incarnate Word, received through faith, the sacraments and ascetic life.
traditions/oriental-orthodox/profile/sac: Seven mysteries: baptism, chrismation, Eucharist, confession, unction of the sick, matrimony and priesthood.
traditions/oriental-orthodox/profile/esc: Resurrection of the body, Christ's return and final judgment; prayers for the departed.
traditions/oriental-orthodox/profile/gov: Episcopal and autocephalous, each church led by its own patriarch or catholicos.
traditions/oriental-orthodox/profile/wor: Ancient liturgies (e.g. of St Basil, St James, the Armenian Divine Liturgy) with extensive fasting calendars.
traditions/oriental-orthodox/profile/can: Broad Old Testament canon including deuterocanonical books; the Ethiopian church has the widest canon, including Enoch and Jubilees.
traditions/oriental-orthodox/status: Active; c. 60 million members (estimates vary widely, especially for Ethiopia).
